title: Merrick Homeland and Historical Boundary Maps
summary: Native communities on western Long Island were connected through neighboring villages, kinship, and shared landscapes.
address_label: Merrick regional history; no identified western-boundary site
ancestral_territory_note: Merrick history includes relationships with neighboring Native communities across western Long Island.
why_this_matters: Maps can make connected communities appear separate. The histories of villages and their relationships help us understand a homeland as a place of movement, kinship, and shared life.
introduction_content:
In The Thirteen Tribes of Long Island: The History of a Myth, historian John A. Strong describes the village connections and overlapping territories obscured by familiar maps of thirteen neatly separated tribes.

Merrick history is part of this wider network of neighboring communities. Rivers, bays, and travel routes connected people across the lines later drawn on maps.
whereintheworld_content: The Native American Greenway marker at Lister Park introduces Merikoke, Rockaway, Canarsie, and Massapequa histories beside the Mill River in Rockville Centre.
